Welcome. Everything on this page runs real R, right inside your browser. Nothing to install, and you cannot break anything. If a line produces an error, that is normal: read it, adjust, and run again.

The first time you click **Run Code**, your browser downloads R once (a few seconds). After that it is quick.

::: {.callout-note}
## The two ideas behind almost every line of R

Writing R comes down to just two things.

An **object** is a named box that stores something. You make one with the arrow `<-`.

```r
x <- 9      # the name x now holds the value 9
```

A **function** is a named command that takes an input and hands back a result. You use it by putting the input in parentheses.

```r
sqrt(9)     # the sqrt function takes 9 and returns 3
```

You can also run a function on an **object** you already made. R reads the name, finds what is stored there, and uses that as the input.

```r
sqrt(x)     # same idea: sqrt takes x (which is 9) and returns 3
```

That is the whole game: you store things in **objects**, and you act on them with **functions**. Everything below is practice with those two moves.
:::

## 1. Make three objects of your own

Fill in the editor with **your own** object names and values. Make two numbers and one sentence (text in quotes).

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: make_three_objects
# a number object:

# another number object:

# a sentence object (use quotes):
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Object names cannot begin with a digit or contain spaces. R is case-sensitive: `MyVar` and `myvar` are different names.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="make_three_objects"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Pick any names you like (for example `score_a`, `score_b`, `motto`) and any values. Numbers go in without quotes; sentences need quotes:

```r
score_a <- 42
score_b <- 7
motto <- "Science is cool."
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="make_three_objects"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

Any valid answer works as long as the names and values are yours. For example:

```r
score_a <- 42
score_b <- 7
motto <- "Science is cool."
```

Nothing prints when you assign — that is expected. The values are stored quietly until you use them.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: make_three_objects
#| check: true
objs <- mget(ls(envir = .envir_result), envir = .envir_result)
nums <- Filter(function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1, objs)
chrs <- Filter(function(v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1, objs)
example_names <- c("number1", "number2", "sentence1")
example_nums <- c(3.14, 11)
example_sentence <- "This is a sentence."
used_example_names <- any(names(objs) %in% example_names)
used_example_vals <- any(vapply(nums, function(v) v %in% example_nums, logical(1))) ||
  any(vapply(chrs, function(v) identical(v, example_sentence), logical(1)))
if (length(nums) < 2) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "I need at least two objects that hold single numbers. Replace the comment prompts with assignments like `score_a <- 42`."
  )
} else if (length(chrs) < 1) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Almost there — add a sentence object too. Put the text inside double quotes so R treats it as character data, not a number."
  )
} else if (used_example_names || used_example_vals) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Pick your own object names and values — do not reuse the assignment examples (`number1`, `number2`, `sentence1`, `3.14`, `11`, or `\"This is a sentence.\"`)."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0(
      "Nice. You created ",
      length(nums),
      " number object(s) and ",
      length(chrs),
      " sentence object(s). They stay in memory for the next steps."
    )
  )
}
```

## 2. Add your two numbers

Use the **names you chose** in Part 1. Add your two number objects together with `+`, then click **Run Code**.

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: add_two_numbers
# Add your two number objects (use the names from Part 1):
```

::: {.hint exercise="add_two_numbers"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Type the names of your two number objects with a plus sign between them. If you named them `score_a` and `score_b`:

```r
score_a + score_b
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="add_two_numbers"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

Use whatever names you picked in Part 1:

```r
score_a + score_b
```

R looks up each name, finds the numbers stored there, and returns their sum.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: add_two_numbers
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
objs <- mget(ls(envir = .envir_result), envir = .envir_result)
nums <- Filter(function(v) is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 1, objs)
if (length(nums) < 2) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Go back to Part 1 and create two number objects first."
  )
} else if (!grepl("\\+", code)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `+` to add your two number objects together — type their names, not the raw numbers."
  )
} else {
  expected <- sum(unlist(nums))
  got <- .last_value
  if (is.numeric(got) && length(got) == 1 && !is.na(got) && abs(got - expected) < 1e-9) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = paste0("That's ", got, ". R looked up your two objects and added the values stored in them.")
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "Make sure you are adding the two number objects you created in Part 1, using their names."
    )
  }
}
```

## 3. Break it on purpose

Now try adding **both numbers and your sentence object** in one line. Run it and read the error message.

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: mix_types_error
# Add both numbers and your sentence object:
```

::: {.hint exercise="mix_types_error"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Use the same three object names from Part 1, joined with `+`:

```r
score_a + score_b + motto
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="mix_types_error"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
score_a + score_b + motto
```

You should see an error like `non-numeric argument to binary operator`. That is the point — R knows how to add numbers, but it will not silently combine a number with a sentence.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why did this happen?

`+` is defined for numbers: R adds the values. A sentence in quotes is **character** data, not a number. When R hits `number + "text"`, it stops and tells you the second argument is not numeric. Errors are information, not failure — read the message and adjust.
:::

## 4. Print your sentence

In R, typing an object's name by itself and running the line shows what is stored there — for a sentence object, you will see the text in the output (often with `[1]` in front, which just means "first item"). That works, but here we want you to practice calling a **function**: put your sentence object's name inside `print()`.

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: print_sentence
print()
```

::: {.hint exercise="print_sentence"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Typing the object name alone (for example `motto`) also shows the sentence — try it if you like. For this step, use `print()` with the name inside the parentheses:

```r
print(motto)
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="print_sentence"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
print(motto)
```

`print()` is a function that takes an object and shows it in the output panel. Typing the name alone does the same thing here; `print()` is just the explicit, named way to ask R to display a value.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| envir: own_objects
#| exercise: print_sentence
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
objs <- mget(ls(envir = .envir_result), envir = .envir_result)
chrs <- Filter(function(v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1, objs)
if (length(chrs) < 1) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "Go back to Part 1 and create a sentence object first."
  )
} else if (!grepl("print\\s*\\(", code)) {
  if (is.character(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = paste0(
        "You got the right text — typing an object name alone shows what is stored (here, \"",
        .last_value,
        "\"). For this step, wrap that name in `print(...)`, for example `print(yo)`."
      )
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "error",
      message = "Type your sentence object's name inside `print(...)`, for example `print(motto)`. (Typing the name alone also shows the value — but here we are practicing the function.)"
    )
  }
} else if (is.character(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0("There it is: \"", .last_value, "\". You called a function on an object you made yourself.")
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Use `print()` with the name of your sentence object from Part 1."
  )
}
```

## 5. Load a package, meet the penguins

Real datasets often live in **packages** — bundles of code and data other people wrote. `library()` switches a package on. Run this to load `palmerpenguins` and peek at the data.

```{webr}
library(palmerpenguins)
head(penguins)
```

Every row is one penguin. Every column is one measurement or label. `head()` is a *function* that shows the first few rows so you are not flooded with all 344 at once.

## 6. Inspect the structure

`str()` is a function that summarizes a dataset: how many rows, how many columns, and the type of each column. Run it on `penguins`.

```{webr}
str(penguins)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check yourself

From the `str()` output, answer these in your head (or jot them down):

1. How many **rows** (penguins) are in the dataset?
2. How many **columns** (variables) does it have?
3. What **type** is the `species` column?

**Answers:** 344 rows; 8 columns; `species` is a `Factor` (R's way of storing categories like Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo).
:::

## 7. Pull a column into an object

You pull one column out of a dataset with a dollar sign: `penguins$body_mass_g` means "the `body_mass_g` column from `penguins`." Store it in an object named `body_mass` by typing the column name after the `$`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: make_column_object
body_mass <- penguins$
```

::: {.hint exercise="make_column_object"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The column is called `body_mass_g`. It goes right after the dollar sign:

```r
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="make_column_object"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
```

Now `body_mass` holds all 344 body-mass values (grams). Some are `NA`, meaning that penguin was never weighed — we will deal with that next.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: make_column_object
#| check: true
if (!exists("body_mass", envir = .envir_result, inherits = FALSE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "warning",
    message = "I don't see an object called `body_mass` yet. Type `body_mass_g` after the `$` so the line reads `body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g`."
  )
} else {
  v <- get("body_mass", envir = .envir_result)
  ref <- if (exists("penguins", envir = .envir_result)) {
    get("penguins", envir = .envir_result)$body_mass_g
  } else {
    NULL
  }
  if (!is.null(ref) && identical(v, ref)) {
    list(
      correct = TRUE,
      type = "success",
      message = "That's it. `body_mass` now holds all 344 body-mass measurements, ready to use by name."
    )
  } else if (is.numeric(v) && length(v) == 344) {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "info",
      message = "That's a real column from penguins, but not the one we're after. Use `body_mass_g`."
    )
  } else {
    list(
      correct = FALSE,
      type = "error",
      message = "Not quite. Take the `body_mass_g` column out of `penguins` with a dollar sign: `body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g`."
    )
  }
}
```

## 8. Summarize with `mean()` — and the `NA` surprise

`mean()` returns the average. Run this as-is and notice what comes back.

```{webr}
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
mean(body_mass)
```

`NA` means "missing." Two penguins in this dataset were never weighed, so R refuses to average around a hole unless you tell it otherwise. Add `na.rm = TRUE` (read: "remove NAs") to skip missing values.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: mean_with_na
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: mean_with_na
mean(body_mass, na.rm = )
```

::: {.hint exercise="mean_with_na"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Type `TRUE` after `na.rm =`:

```r
mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="mean_with_na"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
```

You should see a real number — the average body mass in grams, ignoring the two missing penguins.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: mean_with_na
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
if (!grepl("na\\.rm\\s*=\\s*TRUE", code, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Type `TRUE` after `na.rm =` so the line reads `mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`."
  )
} else if (is.numeric(.last_value) && length(.last_value) == 1 && !is.na(.last_value)) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = paste0(
      "Average body mass: ",
      round(.last_value, 1),
      " g. R skipped the missing values and computed the mean of the rest."
    )
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Make sure `body_mass` is loaded and you set `na.rm = TRUE`."
  )
}
```

## 9. Turn your object into a labeled plot

`hist()` draws a **histogram** — a picture of how often each range of values shows up. Add a title and axis label inside the quotes.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: plot_column
body_mass <- penguins$body_mass_g
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: plot_column
hist(body_mass,
     main = "",
     xlab = "")
```

::: {.hint exercise="plot_column"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Any descriptive title and label work. For example:

```r
hist(body_mass,
     main = "Penguin body mass",
     xlab = "g")
```
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="plot_column"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
hist(body_mass,
     main = "Penguin body mass",
     xlab = "g")
```

Most penguins cluster around 3,000–4,500 g, with a long tail toward heavier birds.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: plot_column
#| check: true
code <- paste(.user_code, collapse = "\n")
made_hist <- grepl("hist\\s*\\(", code)
used_obj  <- grepl("body_mass", code)
has_main  <- grepl("main\\s*=", code)
has_xlab  <- grepl("xlab\\s*=", code)
if (made_hist && used_obj && has_main && has_xlab) {
  list(
    correct = TRUE,
    type = "success",
    message = "Beautiful. You turned a column of numbers into a labeled picture — title, axis, and all."
  )
} else if (made_hist && used_obj && (!has_main || !has_xlab)) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Add both `main = \"...\"` (plot title) and `xlab = \"...\"` (x-axis label) inside `hist(...)`."
  )
} else if (made_hist && !used_obj) {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "info",
    message = "Plot `body_mass` inside `hist(...)`."
  )
} else {
  list(
    correct = FALSE,
    type = "error",
    message = "Use `hist(body_mass, main = \"...\", xlab = \"...\")` with your own title and label text."
  )
}
```

## 10. Recap — you already wrote the whole script

If you ran every step above in order, you already executed the core of Coding Assignment 1. Here is the full five-line script from the assignment, using `penguin_data` instead of `data` (both work; `data` is also a built-in R function name, so many people avoid it):

```r
library(palmerpenguins)
penguin_data <- penguins
str(penguin_data)
mean(penguin_data$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
hist(penguin_data$body_mass_g, main = "Penguin body mass", xlab = "g")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What does each line do?

1. **`library(palmerpenguins)`** — Loads the package so the `penguins` dataset becomes available.
2. **`penguin_data <- penguins`** — Copies the dataset into a shorter object name you can reuse.
3. **`str(penguin_data)`** — Prints the structure: 344 rows, 8 columns, and the type of each column.
4. **`mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)`** — Computes the average body mass in grams, skipping penguins with missing weights.
5. **`hist(...)`** — Draws a histogram of body mass with a title and x-axis label.

If you can explain each line in your own words, you are ready for the graded assignment on Canvas.
:::

## Keep playing

No grading here, and no wrong answer. Try making a different column into an object and plotting it. What does flipper length look like?

```{webr}
flipper_length <- penguins$flipper_length_mm
hist(flipper_length, main = "Flipper length", xlab = "mm")
```

Curious how two measurements relate? This draws one penguin per point, flipper length against body mass:

```{webr}
plot(penguins$flipper_length_mm, penguins$body_mass_g)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Try this with a partner.** One of you predicts what a plot will look like before running it; the other runs it. Then compare what you saw to what you expected, and swap. Saying your prediction out loud first is one of the fastest ways to learn.
:::
